formation.title: The Kingdom of the Lombards
formation.text:
In the basilica at Monza the Corona Ferrea is lifted from Theodolinda's treasury: a band of gold and gems closed, so the canons swear, around a nail of the True Cross. Since the days of the Lombard kings, whoever would rule Italy has knelt for this crown at Pavia or Monza; Frederick Barbarossa wore it, and it broke against the Carroccio at Legnano all the same. Now the cities of the plain answer to one lord again, from the armouries of Milan to the rice water of the Lomellina.

But two memories contend for this kingdom. The Visconti built a state above the communes: chancery, castle and crown, a duchy that dealt with kings as an equal. And against it stands the older oath: Pontida, the League, the commune of Sant'Ambrogio that governed Milan for three years without a duke and called itself golden. A crown of iron, or a republic of saints and citizens: the regnum must choose what it is.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

modifiers.name: The Iron Crown
modifiers.text: The Corona Ferrea has been taken up in the Visconti manner: a crowned state above the communes, with chancery, castle and standing army.

modifiers.name: The Ambrosian Commune
modifiers.text: The oath of Pontida renewed: the cities of the plain govern themselves under Saint Ambrose, and their militias, purses and building yards answer gladly.

advances.name: The Lombard League
advances.text: At Pontida the communes swore their oath, and at Legnano in 1176 their militias around the Carroccio broke the army of Frederick Barbarossa. The Peace of Constance sealed the liberties of the Lombard cities.

advances.name: The Iron Crown
advances.text: The Corona Ferrea of Monza, gold closed around what tradition holds to be a nail of the True Cross. From the Lombard kings to Charles V and Napoleon, whoever would rule Italy sought this crown.

advances.name: The Ambrosian Rite
advances.text: Milan keeps the liturgy of Saint Ambrose: its own chant, its own calendar, its own carnival ending days after everyone else's. Popes have tried to Romanize it and failed; the rite is the city.

advances.name: The Marcite
advances.text: The Cistercians of Chiaravalle learned to flood meadows with a moving film of spring water, so the grass grew green under winter frost. Cattle fed year round: the foundation of Lombard dairy wealth.

advances.name: The Milanese Armourers
advances.text: Around the Via degli Spadari the armourers' guilds of Milan hammered Lombard iron into harness for half of Europe. From these workshops the Missaglia dynasty would rise.

advances.name: The Comacine Masters
advances.text: The itinerant master builders of the Como lakes, organized in lodges since Lombard times, raised churches, towers and walls across Italy and beyond. To build in stone was a Lombard export.

advances.name: Missaglia Harness
advances.text: Tommaso and Antonio Missaglia made Milan's white armour the finest in Europe, exported from Spain to Flanders. A man-at-arms in Milanese plate feared neither lance nor bolt.

advances.name: Resident Ambassadors
advances.text: Francesco Sforza's chancery kept permanent envoys at friendly courts, the first resident embassies in Europe. Milan learned of every scheme in Italy before the schemers had finished dinner.

advances.name: The Ca' Granda
advances.text: In 1456 Francesco Sforza founded the Ospedale Maggiore, merging Milan's scattered hospices into one great house of care with a rational plan by Filarete: civic medicine on a scale Europe had not seen.

advances.name: The Castle at Porta Giovia
advances.text: The Visconti raised a citadel at Porta Giovia and the Sforza rebuilt it grander after the republic tore it down: ducal power in stone, aimed as much at Milan as at Milan's enemies.

advances.name: The Lombard Banks
advances.text: From London's Lombard Street to the fairs of Champagne, 'Lombard' meant lender. At home the Franciscans answered usury with the Monte di Pieta, the charitable bank of 1483.

event.title: The Monte di Pieta
event.text: The word 'Lombard' has meant moneylender from London's Lombard Street to the pawnshops of Bruges: for two centuries the bankers of Milan, Asti and Chieri have carried Lombard credit across Europe, and grown hated for it. Now Franciscan preachers raise a rival from the pulpit: the Monte di Pieta, a charitable bank endowed by the faithful, lending small sums against pledges at little or no interest, so that a poor artisan need not sell his tools to a usurer. Milan's Monte opens in 1483 to the friars' sermons and the bankers' cold fury. The crown must decide whose institution this age belongs to.

modifiers.name: Franciscan Charity
modifiers.text: The Monte di Pieta endowed: credit for the poor, peace in the streets, and the friars preaching gratitude.

modifiers.name: The Piazza of the Banks
modifiers.text: The Lombard banking houses shielded: cheap credit for the crown and merchants who lend to half of Europe.

advances.name: The Navigli
advances.text: The Naviglio Grande reached Milan in 1272; Bertola da Novate cut the Martesana from the Adda in seven years; Leonardo's miter locks joined the levels. No city in Europe commanded such waters.

event.title: The Engineer at the Locks
event.text: A Florentine engineer in ducal service walks the towpath of the Martesana, sketchbook in hand. Bertola da Novate cut this canal from the Adda in seven years; the Naviglio Grande has watered the plain for two centuries; and where the two systems meet, the levels refuse to agree. The engineer proposes gates hung in pairs, meeting in a shallow V against the current, so that the water itself seals them: a miter lock, drawn in his notebook beside siege engines, bombards and a bronze horse for the duke. The same hand offers the state mastery of water or mastery of war, and the chancery must set him a commission.

modifiers.name: Waters and Locks
modifiers.text: The engineer set to the canals: miter locks, level basins, and a plain that builds and grows.

options.text: Set him to the engines of war

modifiers.name: Military Engineering
modifiers.text: The engineer set to war: bastions surveyed, bombards cast, sieges pressed with method.

advances.name: The Rice Estates
advances.text: Under the Sforza, rice took root in the flooded fields of the Lomellina and spread along the canals. The low plain became Europe's rice bowl, and the risaia its signature landscape.

advances.name: The Peace of Lodi
advances.text: In 1454, in a Lombard town, Milan and Venice ended their wars and the Italic League was born: forty years of balance, the first equilibrium system in European diplomacy.

event.title: The Peace of Lodi
event.text: In April 1454, in the small Lombard town of Lodi, exhausted envoys set their seals to a peace that ended decades of war between Milan and Venice. Within months it grew into the Italic League: Milan, Venice, Florence, the Pope and Naples bound to keep the peninsula's balance, the first such system Europe had seen. For forty years the peace of Lodi held, and in its shade the peninsula grew rich and brilliant. The question every chancery now debates is what a balance is for: is equilibrium the achievement itself, or merely the quiet in which a prudent state sharpens its sword?

modifiers.name: The Italian Equilibrium
modifiers.text: The Italic League upheld: the balance of Lodi keeps the peninsula's peace and its roads busy.

modifiers.name: An Armed Peace
modifiers.text: The quiet years of Lodi spent sharpening the sword: cheap armies, fast musters, watchful spies.

advances.name: The Brescian Gunsmiths
advances.text: In Gardone Val Trompia the forges turned valley iron into gun barrels; Bartolomeo Beretta's workshop was already casting them in 1526. Brescian barrels armed Venice and half the Mediterranean.

advances.name: The Paper Valley of Garda
advances.text: Along the Toscolano gorge, sixty water-driven mills beat linen rags into paper. The valley of the paper mills supplied the presses of Venice, and its merchants sold Lombard paper across Europe.

advances.name: The Borromean Reform
advances.text: Carlo Borromeo made Milan the working model of the Counter-Reformation: the seminary of 1564 among the first in Europe, synods, visitations and a clergy that could finally read what it preached.

event.title: The Shepherd of the Plague
event.text: In 1576 the plague enters Milan, and the governor and the great families flee. The archbishop stays. Carlo Borromeo empties his household to feed the quarantined, organizes the parishes into a machinery of relief, and walks barefoot through the dying city with a relic of the Holy Nail, a rope around his neck like a condemned man, offering himself for his people. The lazzaretto fills, the ordinances hold, and Milan learns that a state can fight a pestilence rather than merely endure it. They will call it San Carlo's plague, as if the sickness itself had been conquered by its shepherd.

options.text: The shepherd stays with the flock

modifiers.name: The Shepherd of the Plague
modifiers.text: The archbishop stayed when the governor fled: relief organized parish by parish, and a people that trusts its church.

advances.name: The Biblioteca Ambrosiana
advances.text: Federico Borromeo opened his library in 1609 to any reader who could use it, with agents buying manuscripts from Greece to the Levant: one of the first public libraries in Europe.

advances.name: The Armoury of Europe
advances.text: From the Italian Wars to the Thirty Years' War, Milanese and Brescian workshops armed the armies of kings. Whoever held Lombardy held the arsenal of the south.

advances.name: Sanitation of State
advances.text: The Lazzaretto of 1488, the health passes, the plague ordinances of 1576 and 1630: Milan built a public machinery against pestilence that few states matched.

advances.name: The Luthiers of Cremona
advances.text: Amati taught Guarneri and Stradivari, and a few streets of Cremona set the sound of European music. No instrument since has escaped comparison with theirs.

event.title: The Workshops of Cremona
event.text: In a few streets of Cremona, within sound of each other's hammers, the workshops of Amati, Guarneri and Stradivari are perfecting an instrument. Spruce from the alpine valleys, maple, and a varnish whose secret will be argued over for centuries: from these a bottega of a dozen hands produces violins that courts from Madrid to Vienna bid against each other to own. No throne commissioned this supremacy; it grew from a town of luthiers in the Lombard plain, and while the workshops thrive, the name of Cremona is worth an embassy.

modifiers.name: Golden Age of Lutherie
modifiers.text: The workshops of Cremona at their zenith: every court in Europe bids for a Lombard violin.

advances.name: The Theresian Censimento
advances.text: Begun in 1718 and completed in 1760 under Pompeo Neri, the Lombard cadastre measured and valued every parcel of land in the state: the most exact survey in Europe, and the end of taxation by privilege.

event.title: The Census Completed
event.text: Begun in 1718 and finished at last in 1760 under Pompeo Neri's direction, the censimento has measured every field, orchard and mulberry row in Lombardy: tens of thousands of maps, each parcel valued, each owner entered in the registers. No state in Europe knows its own land so exactly. The implications are quietly revolutionary: if the register is the only measure, then the palace pays by the same rule as the farm, and the patrician exemptions that have hollowed the treasury for two centuries have no page to hide on. The great families understand this perfectly, which is why they are already at the minister's door.

options.text: One measure for palace and farm

modifiers.name: The Just Cadastre
modifiers.text: The registers published and enforced: one measure for palace and farm, and a treasury that stands on fact.

modifiers.name: Pact with the Patriciate
modifiers.text: The census softened for the great houses: their dignities kept, their loyalty secured, the court's standing enhanced.

advances.name: The Valtellina Terraces
advances.text: On dry-stone terraces above the Adda, mountain vineyards produced wine that crossed the passes to Swiss and Austrian tables: the alpine trade of a landlocked kingdom.

advances.name: The Ville di Delizia
advances.text: The patriciate of Milan built its pleasure villas on the lakes and in the countryside: Villa d'Este at Cernobbio and a hundred kin, splendour rooted in the soil of the estates.

advances.name: The Lombard Enlightenment
advances.text: The Verri brothers' journal Il Caffe and Beccaria's Dei delitti e delle pene made Milan a capital of reform. Europe rewrote its penal codes against a Lombard argument.

event.title: Il Caffe
event.text: In Milan the brothers Pietro and Alessandro Verri gather economists, jurists and wits around a journal named for the coffee house where such arguments live: Il Caffe. From this circle in 1764 comes a small book by the young Cesare Beccaria, Dei delitti e delle pene, which argues with terrible calm that torture proves nothing and that the gallows degrades the law that raises it. Within a generation it is quoted in Petersburg, Philadelphia and Paris; empresses and republics alike will rewrite their codes against it. A Lombard coffee table has become a tribunal for the penal law of Europe.

modifiers.name: The Lombard Lights
modifiers.text: Il Caffe in every learned hand: the reforming press of Milan argues, and Europe listens.

advances.name: The Ateneo of Pavia
advances.text: Founded in 1361 and reborn under Maria Theresa and Joseph II, the University of Pavia housed Spallanzani's experiments and Volta's laboratory: the scientific engine of Lombardy.

event.title: The Voltaic Pile
event.text: In the physics cabinet at Pavia, Alessandro Volta stacks discs of copper and zinc between brine-soaked cloth and closes the circuit: a steady electric current, the first the world has seen, drawn from a pile of metal on a table. The university that Maria Theresa and Joseph II rebuilt has repaid them with a new force of nature. Volta will demonstrate the pile to Napoleon himself, and the unit of every current that will ever flow will carry a Lombard name.

modifiers.name: The Voltaic Pile
modifiers.text: A steady current from a pile of metal discs: Pavia's laboratory has handed the age a new force.

advances.name: The Garden of Europe
advances.text: Travellers agreed that no farmland in the world matched the irrigated Lombard plain: water, rice, wheat and pasture interlocking in a single engineered landscape.

advances.name: The Kingdom of Italy
advances.text: In the Duomo of Milan in 1805, Napoleon set the Iron Crown on his own head: 'God gave it to me, woe to him who touches it.' Milan was the capital of a Kingdom of Italy once more.

destiny.name: Il Regno Italico
destiny.text: The regnum Italicum: the kingdom of the plain that the Corona Ferrea has implied since the Lombard kings. Hold the realm steady and its restoration can begin.

event.title: The Course of the Regnum
event.text:
The coronation is done, the realm is quiet, and the chanceries of Europe have begun to write the old words again: regnum Italicum, the kingdom of the Lombards, dormant since the emperors let it slip. Whoever holds the Corona Ferrea holds an argument older than any living dynasty: that the plain of the Po is not a province of anyone's empire but a kingdom in its own right, with its own crown, its own rite and its own stubborn cities.

What kind of kingdom it is to be, the coronation has already answered. What remains is to make the answer true, league by league and ledger by ledger.

destiny.name: The Scaliger Inheritance
destiny.text: Break the encirclement of the old wars: take Verona and Parma from the heirs of the della Scala lordship, and keep an army of thirty thousand men worthy of a kingdom.

conditions.text: Own Verona, or a subject owns it
Own Parma, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Scaliger Inheritance
event.text:
A generation ago the della Scala of Verona held the widest lordship in the plain, and Milan lived hemmed between Scaliger Parma to the south and Scaliger Verona to the east. That ring is broken. From the Adda to the Adige and south across the Po, the cities that once fenced Milan in now march under her banners.

The men of Verona keep their statutes and their saints; they pay their hearth tax to a Lombard chamber now. Every road out of the plain lies open, and the captains have begun to speak of Tuscany the way merchants speak of a fair.

options.text: From the Adda to the Adige

destiny.name: The Count of Virtù
destiny.text: Follow Gian Galeazzo's road south: bring Bologna and Siena under the Biscione, ring Florence with Lombard garrisons, and hold fifty thousand men under arms to keep what is taken.

conditions.text: Own Bologna, or a subject owns it
Own Siena, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Count of Virtù
event.text:
Bologna has opened its gates and Siena has taken the Biscione's protection. The roads into Tuscany and Romagna answer to Lombard garrisons, and Florence wakes to find herself ringed on three sides, her grain roads watched, her bankers writing nervous letters.

In the castle at Pavia the council weighs two instruments of empire. The jurists point north, to the Empire that still claims to license every crown in Italy: gold paid to an embarrassed King of the Romans buys a diploma that makes conquest lawful and vassalage dignified. The captains point at the map instead: no parchment took Bologna, and a state built by the sword is kept by it.

modifiers.name: The Ducal Diploma
modifiers.text: A great title bought with a mountain of florins: conquest made lawful, vassalage made dignified, and the mint quietly asked to cover the price.

modifiers.name: The Sword of the Biscione
modifiers.text: The state that parchment never built: fast columns, stormed walls, and soldiers who find their courage again overnight.

destiny.name: Rex Italiae
destiny.text: Complete what no Visconti lived to finish: Florence and Rome under the king's peace, an army of seventy five thousand men, and prestige worthy of the Iron Crown.

conditions.text: Own Florence, or a subject owns it
Own Rome, or a subject owns it

event.title: Rex Italiae
event.text:
Florence keeps the king's peace and Rome has received a Lombard garrison with the honors due a protector. Nothing now stands between the Corona Ferrea and the title it has implied for seven centuries. In Theodolinda's basilica at Monza the canons unlock the treasury, and the court must decide what manner of king walks out of it.

One counsel is patient: crown and law, the registers carried into every conquered chamber, Italians made subjects rather than tributaries, until the kingdom is a fact no army needs to restate. The other is Roman in the older sense: kingship as command, the peninsula held by the same iron that won it.

modifiers.name: The Crown at Monza
modifiers.text: Kingship as law: conquered cities entered in the registers, their peoples made subjects, their separatisms starved of grievance.

modifiers.name: Lord of Italy
modifiers.text: Kingship as command: siege trains against every recalcitrant wall, garrisons fed and replaced, and a land that devours invaders.

destiny.name: The Credenza di Sant'Ambrogio
destiny.text: Order the commonwealth's finances as the commune once did: give the Credenza its council hall in Milan and count a thousand ducats of free coin in the common purse.

conditions.text: Milan is held by the commonwealth and has a council hall

event.title: The Credenza of Sant'Ambrogio
event.text:
The commune's elders have revived an old name: the Credenza di Sant'Ambrogio, the sworn council that once spoke for the popolo against the great families. Its business now is arithmetic. The banking houses have been brought inside the walls of the law, the estimo is assessed by parish and published, and the common purse, counted before witnesses in the sacristy of the basilica, holds more than a thousand ducats of free coin.

No duke ordered any of this. The cities of the plain have taxed themselves, as the League once did, and found themselves rich.

destiny.name: The Gate to the Sea
destiny.text: Give the ledgers a coastline: bring Genoa into the commonwealth's system, put silk on the capital's exchange, and double the common purse to two thousand ducats.

conditions.text: Own Genoa, or a subject owns it

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Gate to the Sea
event.text:
Genoa has come into the commonwealth's system, and the commune of Saint Ambrose has what every landlocked ledger dreams of: a port. Lombard silk and fustian go down the mountain roads to the Ligurian quays, where the exchange booths quote Milanese cloth in three currencies.

In the merchant courts two petitions lie side by side. The shipowners ask for keels: a fleet under the commune's flag, so that no Venetian or Catalan convoy can shut the sea road. The bankers ask for fairs: chartered seasons of exchange where bills drawn in Milan settle debts from Bruges to Chios, and the profit of the sea is taken in ink.

modifiers.name: The Way of the Sea
modifiers.text: Keels on the slips and crews on the rolls: the commune's flag goes to sea and intends to be respected there.

modifiers.name: The Exchange Fairs
modifiers.text: Chartered seasons where bills settle debts from Bruges to Chios: the profit of the sea taken in ink, to the Church's loud discomfort.

destiny.name: The Golden Republic
destiny.text: Make the golden name true: Milan built up to twice what it was, a library in Pavia for the jurists who proclaimed the republic, and three thousand ducats in the treasury of the commonwealth.

conditions.text: Milan is held by the commonwealth and has at least 72 development
Pavia is held by the commonwealth and has a library

event.title: The Golden Republic
event.text:
They called the republic of 1447 golden for three desperate years; this one has earned the name. Travellers cross the border and write home in disbelief: canals threaded through rice water, schools in market towns, a treasury that publishes its accounts and holds three thousand ducats against the printed page.

The commonwealth of the Lombard cities is the richest ground in Europe governed by its own citizens, and its council must decide what keeps a golden republic golden. The lawyers offer a constitution: the civic order written down, so that no captain can ever again turn command into a crown. The captains of the gates offer the older answer: walls manned by citizens who own what they defend.

modifiers.name: The Civic Constitution
modifiers.text: The commonwealth written down: councils that legislate briskly, registers on good Lombard paper, and a citizenry too watchful for complacency.

modifiers.name: The Citizen Walls
modifiers.text: The Carroccio's oldest lesson: walls manned by men who own what they defend, garrisons swollen with burghers, and marches that cost the commune little.

units.name: Company of Death
units.text: The sworn guard of the Carroccio in Lombard League tradition: the Company of the Carroccio and the Knights of Death of the chronicles, urban militia oath-bound never to retreat from the standard.

units.name: Uomini d'Arme
units.text: Ducal men-at-arms in full Missaglia harness, the finest plate in Europe. Superbly protected and correspondingly slow and costly to field.

units.name: Royal Italian Guard
units.text: The guard regiments of the Kingdom of Italy, raised in Milan after the Iron Crown coronation of 1805: elite shock infantry committed where the fire is hottest.

buildings.name: Treasury of the Iron Crown
buildings.text: The chapel-treasury of Monza cathedral, where Theodolinda's basilica keeps the Corona Ferrea. Kings of Italy from the Lombards to Napoleon were crowned with it.

buildings.name: Marcita
buildings.text: A Cistercian water meadow: spring water kept moving over the grass so it grows through winter, feeding cattle the whole year.

where.text: The location's raw material is Livestock

buildings.name: Armeria
buildings.text: An armourers' quarter in the Milanese manner, hammering Lombard iron into plate harness for export. The Missaglia workshops armed half of Europe from streets like these.

where.text: Iron is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Ospedale Maggiore
buildings.text: The Ca' Granda: one great civic hospital in place of scattered hospices, in the pattern Francesco Sforza and Filarete set in Milan in 1456.

buildings.name: Castello di Porta Giovia
buildings.text: A ducal citadel in the Visconti-Sforza manner: garrison, armoury and the duke's fist over the city that hosts it.

buildings.name: Monte di Pieta
buildings.text: The Franciscan charitable pawnbank: small loans against pledges at little or no interest, so the poor need not go to the usurer.

buildings.name: Naviglio
buildings.text: A navigable canal with locks and towpaths in the Lombard manner, carrying grain, marble and trade while watering the fields it passes.

buildings.name: Risaia
buildings.text: A flooded rice estate of the low plain, fed by the irrigation network that spread rice from the Lomellina across Lombardy. Where the land grows rice, it yields more of it, and more food.

where.text: The location's raw material is Rice

buildings.name: Cartiera
buildings.text: A water-driven paper mill in the Toscolano pattern, beating linen rags into the rag paper that fed the printing presses of Italy.

where.text: Lumber is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Seminario
buildings.text: A Tridentine seminary on the Borromean model: the diocese trains its own clergy, and the pulpit finally knows its letters.

buildings.name: Ambrosiana
buildings.text: A public library with its own college of doctors, in the pattern Federico Borromeo set in 1609: open to any reader who can use it.

buildings.name: Lazzaretto
buildings.text: A quarantine hospital outside the walls, with health passes and plague ordinances: the sanitary machinery Milan tested in 1576 and 1630.

buildings.name: Bottega Liutaia
buildings.text: A luthier workshop in the Cremonese tradition: alpine spruce, maple and a jealously guarded varnish, sold to courts across Europe.

buildings.name: Villa di Delizia
buildings.text: A patrician pleasure villa on the lakes or among the estates: gardens, galleries and the landlord's presence rooted in the countryside.

buildings.name: Gabinetto di Fisica
buildings.text: A university physics cabinet in the Pavia pattern: instruments, demonstrations and the laboratory where Volta stacked his pile.

buildings.name: Palazzo Reale
buildings.text: The old court beside the Duomo rebuilt as the seat of a crowned kingdom: throne hall, chancery and the apartments of the Rex Italiae.

buildings.name: Broletto Nuovo
buildings.text: The palace of reason on the Piazza dei Mercanti: the bell, the bench and the register, communal government in stone.

list.name: Senato di Milano
list.text: Louis XII erected the Senate by the ordonnance of Vigevano on 11 November 1499, seventeen members on the model of the parlements of France, and every later master of Milan kept it: Sforza, Spanish and Austrian alike. It judged in last instance, its rulings binding on every lower court, and it registered the sovereign's decrees, refusing those it held contrary to the law of the duchy. A seat on its bench was the summit of a Milanese jurist's career. Joseph II stripped its administrative powers in 1771 and abolished it by edict on 11 February 1786.

list.name: Magistrato Straordinario
list.text: The chamber court of the prince's own patrimony, sitting from 1541 under a president and six questors, three of the toga and three of the cape and sword. It administered fiefs and regalia, confiscations and pecuniary condemnations, vacant inheritances, the royal lakes and rivers, and the licensing of exports of essential goods. Left to rot it becomes what Spanish Milan made of it, a counter selling fiefs and the fiscal immunities that came with them. Maria Theresa's edict of 30 April 1749 folded it into the single Magistrato Camerale.

list.name: Regalia delle Acque
list.text: Running water in the duchy belonged to the prince. From the 1490s the Camera Ducale sold and leased it by the ounce, measured at the bocche where a roggia left the Naviglio, and a concession once bought could be resold or rented on. The Naviglio Grande alone was reckoned at 125,000 ducats a year in Leonardo's time. In 1515 Massimiliano Sforza, needing money against the French, sold the waters, beds and banks of the Grande and the Martesana outright to the city of Milan.

list.name: Tribunale di Provvisione
list.text: Milan's own magistracy: twelve citizens whose powers the council fixed on 11 April 1280, presided from 1366 by a Vicar of Provision. It ran the annona, buying grain, setting the weight and price of the loaf, keeping the markets, the streets and the city accounts. In 1515 the city won the right to name 150 deputies who elected the vicar and the twelve. The contado paid for the cheap loaf in requisitions at fixed prices, and when the granaries failed the city rioted anyway, as it did at San Martino in November 1628.

list.name: Ufficio di Sanità
list.text: Milan registered every death from 1452, each corpse seen by a physician of the health office and reported by the officiali delle bollette in the parishes. The Lazzaretto rose outside Porta Orientale from 1488, 280 rooms around a court almost 400 metres on a side. Francesco II Sforza raised the office to the Magistrato di Sanità on 13 May 1534, and its health passes, sealed houses and cordons answered the plagues of 1576 and 1630. Merchants hated the quarantine and the archbishop's clergy defied the ban on assemblies. Starved of funds the board stops knowing rather than stops policing: 1630 ended in the hunt for the untori.

list.name: Scuole della Dottrina Cristiana
list.text: Castellino da Castello opened a Sunday school at San Giacomo in Porta Nuova in 1536 and taught the children of the poor their catechism together with reading, writing and arithmetic. His Compagnia of 1539 spread the model: fifteen schools when Ormaneto came as vicar general in 1564, twice as many within two years, thirty at Castellino's death. Carlo Borromeo gave the congregation San Dalmazio in 1577 and set the Oblates of Saint Ambrose over it. The Ambrosian church taught Lombardy its letters parish by parish, answering to the archbishop and not to the governor.
